contentHtml:
How product recommendations work for a small online store

In short: A small Indian online store does not need a machine learning team for product recommendations. Shopify's free Search & Discovery app and WooCommerce's built-in up-sells and cross-sells cover most of it. Start with hand-picked pairs and bestsellers, let the platform's automatic "related" suggestions fill gaps, and build a custom engine only when you have the order history to feed it.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against Shopify's and WooCommerce's documentation and the research listed at the end. I name no conversion uplift figures, because I found none from a source I would trust for a small Indian store.

The old version of this post was about the cold-start problem. That is still the heart of it. A small store is permanently in cold start: few orders, new products every season, and many customers who visit once. Every choice below follows from that.

Your options at a glance

Here is what each route gives you and what it needs from you.

Ways a small Indian store can show product recommendations

RouteWhat it doesWhat the official docs sayNeeds
Shopify Search & Discovery appRelated and complementary products on product pagesListed as Free, developed by Shopify; adds related and complementary products on product detail pagesA Shopify store; Shopify Network Intelligence enabled for some features
Shopify related recommendationsAutomatic suggestionsOnly related recommendations are auto-generated by ShopifyNothing beyond the theme supporting it
Shopify complementary recommendationsHand-picked "goes well with" itemsComplementary recommendations need to be manually set upYour time, product by product
WooCommerce up-sells and cross-sellsAlternatives on the product page, add-ons in the cartUp-sells are recommended instead of the viewed product; cross-sells are complementary products based on the cartSet in each product's Linked Products tab
WooCommerce related productsAutomatic suggestionsGenerated from categories or tags shared with the product being viewedClean categories and tags
Custom enginePersonalised suggestions per customerItem-to-item collaborative filtering, as described by Amazon in 2003Enough order history and a developer

Source: Shopify App Store and Shopify developer docs and Shopify Help Center and WooCommerce docs and IEEE Internet Computing, read 16 November 2026.

For most stores I would stop at the first four rows for a long time. The last row is where the cold-start problem bites hardest.

What cold start means for a small store

Google's machine learning course on recommendation systems defines it plainly. If an item is not seen during training, "the system can't create an embedding for it," and "This issue is often called the cold-start problem." In shop terms: a model that learns from past orders knows nothing about a product nobody has bought yet, or a customer who has never ordered.

Google's suggested workaround for items with no interactions is a heuristic: approximate them "by averaging the embeddings of items from the same category." In plain words, treat a new kurta like the other kurtas in its category until it has its own sales. That is what WooCommerce's related products already do in a simpler way, using shared categories and tags.

A small Indian store faces cold start on three fronts at once:

  • New products. A festive collection launches three weeks before Diwali and is gone after. It never builds history.
  • New customers. Most visitors arrive from an Instagram or Meta ad, see one product and leave. There is no history to personalise from.
  • Thin orders. A few hundred orders a month, many with a single item, give very few "bought together" pairs to learn from.

The approach that works when data is thin

The idea behind most store recommendations is older than many founders realise. Amazon's 2003 paper in IEEE Internet Computing described "item-to-item collaborative filtering": instead of finding similar customers, it compares similar items. The abstract says its online computation "scales independently of the number of customers and number of items in the product catalog."

For a small store, the useful lesson is the item-to-item idea, not the scale. "People who bought this also bought that" needs pairs of products in the same orders. Until you have enough of those pairs, you fill the gap with three things you already know:

  • Your own knowledge of what goes together. A saree with a matching blouse piece. A face wash with a moisturiser from the same range. This is exactly what Shopify's complementary recommendations and WooCommerce's cross-sells are for.
  • Your catalogue structure. Category, fabric, price band, occasion. Good tags make the automatic "related" suggestions sensible.
  • Bestsellers. When you know nothing about a visitor, showing what sells is a reasonable default, and it needs no model at all.

As orders grow, let the data take over for products with real history, and keep the hand-picked pairs for new launches.

Setting it up on Shopify

Shopify's developer documentation explains the split. "Only related recommendations are auto-generated by Shopify." "Complementary recommendations need to be manually set up," and both "can be configured using the Shopify Search & Discovery app." The Product Recommendations API accepts an intent of related or complementary, with related as the default, and returns between 1 and 10 products.

The Search & Discovery app's App Store listing shows it as Free and developed by Shopify, with features including product recommendations and "Add related and complementary products on product detail pages." The Help Center notes one requirement for some of its features: "Using this feature requires Shopify Network Intelligence to be enabled in your privacy settings."

Setting it up on WooCommerce

WooCommerce has three built-in kinds, described in its documentation:

  • Up-sells: "products that you recommend instead of the product a customer is viewing," such as a premium version.
  • Cross-sells: "complementary products that you recommend based on items in a customer’s cart."
  • Related products: WooCommerce "automatically generates related products based on categories or tags shared with the product being viewed." You cannot pick them by hand. To influence them, the docs say to "group similar products in the same category or give them the same tags."

Up-sells and cross-sells are set in each product's Linked Products tab. For a store with a few hundred products, that is an afternoon's work for the bestsellers, and it covers most of the traffic.

How to set up recommendations, step by step

Step 1. Clean your catalogue first. Consistent categories, tags for fabric, size range, skin type or occasion, and a price band. Automatic related suggestions on both platforms lean on this structure.

Step 2. List your top 30 products by sales. These get most of the page views. Everything you do by hand starts here.

Step 3. Hand-pick two or three companions for each. Things a customer genuinely needs with it, or a sensible next item. On Shopify these are complementary products in Search & Discovery; on WooCommerce they are cross-sells.

Step 4. Add one up-sell where it is honest. A larger pack, a better fabric, a combo. Not a product twice the price that does the same thing.

Step 5. Decide placement. Product page for related and complementary items. Cart page for small add-ons. Keep it to one row on mobile, which is where most Indian shoppers browse.

Step 6. Give new launches a home. For a new collection with no sales, link each new product to two established bestsellers by hand, and tag it so automatic suggestions place it next to similar items.

Step 7. Measure clicks and add-to-cart from the recommendation row. Both platforms' themes or apps can report clicks. The Search & Discovery listing mentions recommendation performance analytics. Compare against the period before.

Step 8. Review every season. Remove companions that are out of stock or discontinued. An out-of-stock recommendation is worse than none.

Where recommendations earn their place

Placement matters as much as the logic. These are the spots I would use, in order of effort.

  • Product page, below the add to cart button. One row of complementary items ("goes well with") and, further down, one row of related alternatives. Keep the companion row closest to the button, because it adds to the order instead of replacing it.
  • Cart page. Small, cheap add-ons that make sense with what is already in the cart: a blouse stitching service, a travel-size version, a cable with a charger. Large items here distract from checkout.
  • Empty search results. When a search finds nothing, show bestsellers from the closest category instead of a blank page.
  • After the order. An order confirmation or a follow-up message a few weeks later suggesting the next item in the routine. This is where a small store's repeat customers come from, and it needs only the order history you already have.

Leave pop-ups and full-screen offers out. On a phone they hide the product the customer came to see. If you send follow-ups on WhatsApp, use approved templates and only to customers who opted in.

How to tell whether it is working

A small store rarely has enough traffic for a clean A/B test on recommendations, so measure simply and over a full season.

  • Click rate on the row. Of people who saw the recommendation row, how many tapped a product in it. If almost nobody taps, the suggestions are not relevant or the row is badly placed.
  • Add to cart from the row. More useful than clicks, because it shows the suggestion was something people wanted.
  • Items per order. Complementary suggestions should push this up. Compare with the same season last year, not last month, because festive months distort everything.
  • Average order value. Watch it together with items per order. A rise in value with no rise in items usually means up-sells, not cross-sells, are doing the work.

Write the numbers down before you change anything, so there is a baseline to compare against.

Worked examples for three Indian stores

These examples are illustrative. The stores and numbers are invented to show the method, not taken from real clients.

An ethnic wear boutique on Shopify

Say a boutique in Hyderabad sells sarees, kurtas and dupattas, with around 400 products and a new collection each festive season. Most orders are a single item. There are not enough co-purchases for automatic suggestions to be meaningful on new pieces.

The owner sets complementary products for her top 30: blouse pieces, matching dupattas, a jewellery set from a partner. New festive pieces are tagged by fabric and occasion, and each is linked by hand to two bestsellers. The automatic related row fills in the rest. Our page on clothing and fashion apps covers this sector.

A skincare brand on WooCommerce

Say a D2C skincare brand sells 40 products across four ranges. Customers often buy one product, like it, and come back for the rest of the routine. Cross-sells in the cart show the next step of the same range: cleanser to toner to moisturiser. Up-sells on the product page show the combo pack.

Because the catalogue is small and well structured, related products by shared tags (skin type, range) work well from day one. After a year of orders, the brand has enough repeat customers to try "bought after" suggestions in follow-up emails. Our ecommerce development service covers builds like this.

A mobile accessories store with a large catalogue

Say a store sells 3,000 phone cases, chargers and cables across hundreds of phone models. Here hand-picking does not scale, but the structure is strong: every product has a compatible phone model. The recommendation rule is simple: show accessories tagged with the same phone model, bestsellers first.

This store is the first of the three where a custom engine might pay off later, because it has many products, many orders and clear item-to-item pairs (case plus screen guard). Until then, tags and a rule do the job.

The one thing this store must get right is compatibility. A charger recommended for the wrong phone is a return, a bad review and a lost customer. So the model tag is checked on every new product before it goes live, and any product without one is kept out of recommendations entirely. Here the data clean-up is not a nice extra before the real work. It is the recommendation system, and it costs nothing but discipline.

Ways recommendations go wrong

  • Recommending the out-of-stock. The row shows a product the customer cannot buy. Filter by stock.
  • Recommending the same thing. Five nearly identical kurtas under a kurta. Mix in a companion, not only lookalikes.
  • Up-sells that feel like a trick. A product twice the price with no clear reason. Customers notice.
  • Building a model too early. A custom engine on a few hundred orders mostly recommends bestsellers, at the cost of a developer's time.
  • Messy tags. "Cotton", "cotton " and "Cottn" split one group into three, and automatic related products get worse.
  • Ignoring mobile. A grid of eight recommendations that pushes the add to cart button below the fold.
  • Personalising without thinking about consent. Using browsing history to personalise is processing personal data. India's DPDP Act section 6 sets the consent standard, and its notice and consent rules apply from May 2027. Plan for it if you build a personalised engine.

When a custom engine is worth it

I would consider building a custom recommendation engine only when most of these are true:

  • You have a large catalogue where hand-picking is impossible.
  • You have steady order volume, with many orders containing more than one item.
  • You have repeat customers, so there is history per person.
  • You have a developer, or a partner, who can maintain it and measure it.
  • You have already done the catalogue clean-up and hand-picked pairs, and measured them.

Then the classic item-to-item approach is the sensible first model, and Google's cold-start heuristics (borrowing from the same category) handle new items. For apps that need it, our AI and ML development team builds and measures these. On small traffic, measuring the change needs care: see our post on A/B testing with small traffic.

A seasonal checklist

  • Tags and categories are consistent: no duplicates, no typos.
  • Top 30 products each have two or three hand-picked companions.
  • New collection products are linked to established bestsellers.
  • Out-of-stock and discontinued items are removed from every recommendation.
  • The recommendation row shows one line on mobile and does not push the add to cart button down.
  • Clicks and add-to-cart from recommendations are compared with last season.
  • If you personalise using browsing history, your notice and consent flow is ready for the DPDP rules.

If you want recommendations scoped into a new store or app, our ₹3,500 requirement analysis gives you a written scope, fixed quotation and timeline before any build starts (how it works). The store, code and accounts stay in your name.

Frequently asked questions

Does a small online store need a recommendation engine?

Usually not a custom one. Shopify's free Search & Discovery app and WooCommerce's built-in up-sells, cross-sells and related products cover most small stores. Build a custom engine only when you have a large catalogue and enough order history.

What is the cold-start problem in recommendations?

A model that learns from past interactions cannot recommend an item it has never seen. Google's recommendation course says this is often called the cold-start problem, and suggests approximating new items from items in the same category.

Is Shopify Search & Discovery free?

Its Shopify App Store listing shows it as Free and developed by Shopify. It lets you add related and complementary products on product detail pages.

What is the difference between related and complementary products on Shopify?

Related products are similar alternatives and are auto-generated by Shopify. Complementary products go well with the item and need to be manually set up, for example in the Search & Discovery app.

What is the difference between up-sells and cross-sells in WooCommerce?

WooCommerce says up-sells are products you recommend instead of the one being viewed, and cross-sells are complementary products recommended based on items in the cart.

How does WooCommerce choose related products?

Automatically, from categories or tags shared with the product being viewed. You cannot pick them by hand, so clean categories and tags matter.

Do I need consent to personalise recommendations in India?

Personalising from a person's browsing or order history is processing personal data. Where you rely on consent, section 6 of the DPDP Act sets the standard, and the notice and consent rules apply from May 2027. Check your setup with a lawyer.
